title: Navigation cardinality and edge-case checklist
summary: Working checklist and exploratory notes for deciding top-level nav count, sub-route depth limits, and handling permission-driven pruning + odd states (empty lists, long names, deep share links). Includes three quick wireframe variants and a small groomed backlog with priority/estimate guesses.
body:
Status: rough notes — goal is a compact, predictable nav that scales from single-tenant hosted API users to enterprise Dedicated/Private customers. These are intentionally terse points for design/PM/engineering tradeoffs.

Context and constraints:
- Console must support 4 primary user personas: developer (fast path for requests/keys), infra/SRE (capacity, logs), product/ops (rollouts, experiments), security/compliance (audit, keys).
- Customers may pin distinct models/routes; nav should make multi-model workflows discoverable without overwhelming.
- Access controls: many pages must be hidden (pruned) for scoped users; pruned menus should leave no orphaned empty sections.
- Mobile and narrow windows: left rail may collapse to bottom sheet or hamburger. Need graceful degradation for keyboard-first users.
- Performance: menu must not load heavy data; route metadata (name, icon, availability) should be packaged separately and cached.

Cardinality heuristics (how many top-level items):
- Empirical target: 6 +/- 1 top-level items maximizes scanability on medium width. Too few = overloaded subs; too many = cognitive spread.
- If product grows, prefer grouping by activity (Observe, Serve, Configure, Models, Team, Billing) rather than by product surface (hosted/dedicated/private).
- Use feature flags to map persona -> default expanded group.

Depth limits and naming rules:
- Max recommended route depth: 3 levels visible in nav (top, subgroup, leaf). Deep flows should surface via search/command palette rather than nested menus.
- Leaf route labels should avoid >3 words; use micro-subcopy on hover/tooltip if needed.
- Avoid symmetric naming collisions: e.g., 'Settings > API Keys' vs 'Team > API Keys' — prefer canonical placement with cross-links.

Edge cases checklist (must handle):
- Permission-pruned nav: ensure the collapsed parent either hides or surfaces a lightweight placeholder that explains why items missing ("No access to Observability features").
- Empty-state sections: if a top-level group has zero enabled sub-pages, consider removing it from visible nav but keep an entry point from search.
- Long route titles and icons: truncation + full title tooltip + announce for screen readers.
- Deep share links (e.g., /console/project/1234/model/abcd/runs/5678) should map to shallow breadcrumbs and allow fallback to the parent page if user lacks access to an intermediate resource.
- Canary or feature-flagged pages: tenant-specific entries must avoid shifting global item positions — they should appear in an "Experimental" contextual bucket or be listed in the command palette.
- Multi-workspace: provide a small workspace switcher region separate from global nav to avoid mixing scopes.
- Keyboard nav: left/right arrow for expand/collapse; home/end jump to top/bottom; type-to-search within nav.
- Unknown route / 404 inside console: show contextual back-targets: previous valid parent routes + quick actions (open support, open command palette).

Accessibility considerations:
- All nav items must be reachable with single keystroke from command palette; provide aria-expanded/aria-controls on groups.
- Focus trap: when nav is opened in mobile overlay, focus must be contained and returned after close.
- Contrast and touch target size meet AA standards.

Wireframe writeups (quick variants):
- Variant A — 'Condensed Left Rail with Context Pane': left rail 64px collapsed icons; expand on hover/focus to show titles; right-side context pane shows child routes for current selection. Good for dense desktop workflows.
- Variant B — 'Group-Focused Top Strip + Command Palette': minimal left rail (logo + profile), top strip contains group chips (Observe | Serve | Models | Config), command palette primary for navigation. Favours keyboard-heavy users and simplifies mobile adaptation.
- Variant C — 'Adaptive Stack (mobile-first)': bottom condensed tab for 4 primary activities + a more menu; in wide view becomes grouped left rail with inline counts for alerts/activities.

Wireframe micro-notes (what to test):
- A: test hover-to-expand discoverability and accidental expansion rate.
- B: measure time-to-open-for-frequent-tasks for keyboard users vs mouse users.
- C: validate reachable critical tasks (create-run, view-logs, set-keys) within 2 taps on mobile.

Metrics to monitor after rollout:
- Navigation click depth distribution (median target <= 3)
- Command palette usage (target: >= 20% power users)
- Time-to-first-action from console entry (goal: 12s for new users, 6s for returning devs)
- Error/fallback rate for deep-share links -> fallback pages, target < 1%

Backlog grooming (tickets, rough priority + t-shirt estimate):
- NAV-701: implement nav metadata endpoint (priority: high, estimate: 3d)
- NAV-702: permission-prune rules + placeholder states (priority: high, estimate: 4d)
- NAV-715: implement command-palette + indexing (priority: medium, estimate: 5d)
- NAV-719: mobile adaptive layout (priority: medium, estimate: 6d)
- NAV-734: breadcrumb fallback handler for deep-share links (priority: low, estimate: 2d)

Implementation guidance for eng: 
- Provide a single JSON manifest per tenant with stable ordering keys so experiments don't shift indexes for existing users.
- Keep heavy state out of nav rendering path; paginate counts or fetch lazily.
- Expose an events hook for nav interactions to feed analytics (nav_open, group_expand, route_select).

Decision drivers (what to vote on in design review):
- Whether to cap top-level items at 6 or allow dynamic grouping for large enterprise customers. My leaning: standardize to <=7 for consistency, but allow a pinned overflow area for enterprise-only items.
- Whether experimental features should alter nav order; recommended: no — keep separate experimental bucket.

Notes to self / unresolved:
- Need to check console telemetry for current number-of-top-level-items per tenant (ask metrics).
- Confirm SSO role-to-perm mapping with IAM team so we can simulate pruning locally.

Conclusion: prefer a hybrid approach — condensed left rail for familiarity + command palette as the fast-path. Ship nav metadata endpoint first and iterate wireframe A/B tests against task completion metrics.
open_questions: How should nav ordering be surfaced to customers in Dedicated where they expect different priorities?
Do we need a separate analytics dimension for 'nav shifted-by-experiment' to track regressions?
Should workspace switcher be global header or integrated into nav?
